Steam Turbine Barring Gear: Purpose, Start Permissives, Interlock Logic, Auto Engage and Troubleshooting

A hot rotor left standing still will bow within minutes and can rub its seals at the next start. The barring gear, its permissive and interlock logic and a few field checks are what keep the shaft straight.

Rotor bow Start permissives Auto engage logic Barring calculator Troubleshooting

Barring gear keeps a hot turbine rotor turning slowly so it cools and warms evenly. Below is how the gear is built, how the DCS logic engages it and what to check when it refuses to start.

Hello everyone, today we are going to learn how the steam turbine barring gear works, why it is needed and how its start and stop logic is built in the DCS.
Quick Answer

What is steam turbine barring gear and why is it used?

Steam turbine barring gear is a motor driven gear train that turns the turbine rotor slowly, typically 2 to 10 rpm according to EPRI, whenever the machine is hot and off steam. It stops the shaft from bowing as the top and bottom cool at different rates. For example, a rotor turned at 4 rpm for 6 hours completes 1440 revolutions, and most OEMs want at least 4 hours on barring before steam is admitted.

What Is Steam Turbine Barring Gear?

A steam turbine barring gear is a small electric motor, reduction gearbox and engaging pinion that rotate the turbine shaft slowly whenever the rotor is hot and not driven by steam. It keeps the rotor straight during cool down after a trip and during warm up before a start, so the shaft does not bow and rub its seals.

Key Facts
  • EPRI gives a typical turning speed of 2 to 10 rpm for most steam turbines.
  • The control system normally engages the gear automatically when rotor speed reaches zero after a shutdown.
  • Lube oil must be in service, and jacking oil where fitted, before the barring motor can start.
  • Most OEMs ask for at least 4 hours on barring before steam flow is established.

For an instrument or control engineer the hardware is simple, but the steam turbine barring gear logic is not. It ties together the lube oil console, the jacking oil pumps, speed probes, limit switches and the motor starter, and a mistake in any one of them can leave a hot rotor standing still.

Advertisement

Why Is Barring Gear Required in a Steam Turbine?

Barring gear is required because a hot, stationary rotor cools unevenly and bends, and a bent rotor rubs, vibrates and can even lock in its casing. Turning it slowly keeps every part of the shaft passing through the same temperature zones, so it stays straight.

Control.com describes two shapes of this temporary bend. Sagging is a downward bend from gravity combined with heat, while hogging is an upward bend caused by the hotter steam that collects at the top of the casing after a trip.

In a machine where steam is superheated to 540 °C or more, the top of the rotor can stay much hotter than the bottom for hours. If the gear fails to engage, Control.com warns that operators have only a few minutes to fix it before hogging begins, and that a hogged rotor can need extensive repair.

Do You Know?

EPRI notes that excessive temporary bowing can lock the rotor in the casing, and its turning gear guide warns: never attempt to use steam to rotate a locked rotor.

You measure the bow with an eccentricity probe, a non contact eddy current proximity sensor that looks at a smooth shaft surface and reads the slow speed runout. API 670 covers this measurement as part of the machinery protection system.

How Does a Barring Gear Work?

A barring motor drives a worm or helical gearbox, and an engaging pinion on the gearbox output is pushed into mesh with a bull gear on the rotor coupling. Once the pinion is in mesh the motor turns the whole train at a few rpm and keeps turning until the operator or the logic stops it.

The figure shows the parts you will meet on site. A zero speed switch or speed probe watches a toothed wheel on the shaft, and the eccentricity probe sits near the bearing where the bow shows clearly.

The air cylinder that moves the pinion carries an engaged limit switch, and the barring motor sits in the MCC with its own overload and motor protection relay. Jacking oil lifts the rotor on a thin oil film so a small motor can break it away from rest.

Quick Tip

During commissioning, stroke the engage cylinder with the motor isolated and watch the engaged limit switch on the DCS. A switch that makes before the pinion is fully in mesh will let the motor start on half a tooth.

Steam Turbine Barring Gear Logic: Permissives and Interlocks

The logic allows the pinion to engage only at zero speed with lube oil and jacking oil healthy, and allows the motor to start only after the engaged switch confirms mesh. It stops the motor on low lube oil pressure, motor overload or rotor speed rising above barring speed.

SignalRole in logicTypical sourceAction
Lube oil header pressureStart permissive and tripPressure switch or transmitterBlock start, stop motor on low
Jacking oil pressureStart permissivePressure switch per bearingBlock start if low
Rotor at zero speedEngage permissiveZero speed probeAllow pinion to engage
Pinion engagedMotor start permissiveLimit switch on cylinderStart barring motor
Speed above barring speedDisengage and lockoutSpeed probeStop motor, pinion thrown out
Motor current highAlarm and tripMCC current signalAlarm, trip on overload

EPRI states that oil pressure sensing is part of the turning gear starting logic and that the lube oil system must be in service whenever the gear runs. Many plants wire the low lube oil pressure contact as de energize to trip so a broken wire also stops the motor.

1
Turbine trips
Stop valves close and the rotor starts to coast down on its own inertia.
2
Jacking oil starts
The jacking oil pump starts at a set coast down speed. EPRI gives 600 rpm as one example.
3
Zero speed detected
The zero speed probe confirms the shaft has stopped and raises an audible alarm.
4
Permissives checked
Lube oil and jacking oil pressures must be healthy before the engage command.
5
Pinion engages
The air cylinder pushes the pinion into mesh and the engaged limit switch makes.
6
Motor starts
The barring motor starts and the DCS shows the rotor on barring.

Put a watchdog on each step. A TON timer on the engage command, typically set from the OEM stroke time, raises an engage failure alarm if the limit switch does not make in time.

What Is the Speed of Turning Gear?

Most steam turbine turning gears run between 2 and 10 rpm, a range EPRI says is set by the OEM for each machine. Going below about 2 rpm can cause bearing damage, vibration and stick slip of the blades.

2 to 10 rpmTypical barring speed
600 rpmExample jacking oil start
4 hMinimum before steam
29 to 32 °CLube oil during barring

How Long Should a Turbine Stay on Barring?

After a shutdown the rotor stays on barring until the turbine has cooled below the OEM temperature, which can take hours to several days. Before a start, most OEMs ask for at least 4 hours on barring, and during long outages EPRI suggests about 5 hours of rotation each week.

A quick check combines two numbers: how many turns the rotor has made and how close the eccentricity is to its limit. The worked example below uses a rotor at 4 rpm for 6 hours with 38 µm eccentricity against an assumed OEM limit of 50 µm.

Revolutions: N = n × 60 × t
N = 4 × 60 × 6 = 1440 rev
Eccentricity ratio: R = e ÷ limit × 100
R = 38 ÷ 50 × 100 = 76 percent
Time check: 6 h ≥ 4 h, so roll is allowed
Barring Time and Eccentricity Check
Result
1440 revolutions, eccentricity 76 percent of limit, roll permissive OK

Use the OEM limit from your turbine manual, since the 50 µm value here is only an example. If the eccentricity is still above the limit after the minimum time, keep the rotor on barring and trend the reading rather than forcing the start.

Benefits of continuous barring
  • Rotor cools and warms evenly, so it stays straight
  • Eccentricity stays inside the OEM limit for the next start
  • Seals and blade tips avoid rubs at run up
  • Bearings see a steady oil film with jacking oil on
Risks if barring stops
  • Hogging begins within minutes on a hot rotor
  • Rotor can lock in the casing and delay the restart
  • High vibration and seal rubs at the next roll
  • Extended outage for straightening or repair
Do You Know?

EPRI notes that jacking or lift oil pumps are common on units of about 1000 MW and above, and that ALSTOM uses them on turbines above roughly 100 MW.

Barring Gear Troubleshooting

When the barring gear will not engage or start, check the permissives first, then the pinion mechanism, then the motor. The EPRI troubleshooting table follows the same order.

SymptomLikely causeWhat to check
Motor will not startPermissive missingStarting permissive values and inputs, power to starter
Pinion will not engageSpeed, limit or pressure switchSwitch states on DCS, manual engage
Cylinder does not moveNo instrument airAir supply and solenoid valves
Low oil pressure tripLube pump not runningPump status, sight glass flow to bearings
High motor currentRubbing or bowed rotorEccentricity, motor windings, bearing oil

If the motor starts but draws high current, treat it as a warning. EPRI lists excessive eccentricity and degraded motor windings among the checks, and a vibration monitoring trend from the last coast down often shows whether the rotor rubbed.

Myth: Barring gear is a maintenance tool, so it does not need safety attention.
Fact: A hot rotor left standing can lock, so the barring logic protects a very expensive machine.
Myth: Slower barring speed is always gentler on the rotor.
Fact: EPRI warns that speeds below about 2 rpm can damage bearings and cause stick slip.
Myth: If the motor will not start, you can roll the rotor with a little steam.
Fact: EPRI states that steam must never be used to rotate a locked rotor.

Handle any bypass of a barring permissive the way you handle a safety signal bypass, with a permit, a time limit and a log entry. Forcing the engaged switch to start the motor can strip the pinion teeth.

Quick Tip

If the gear trips repeatedly at night, trend lube oil header pressure at one second resolution. A pressure dip at a pump changeover is a common reason the barring motor drops out.

Barring Gear vs Turning Gear: Is There a Difference?

There is no technical difference, since both terms describe the gear that slowly turns a turbine rotor. Barring gear is the common term in India and Europe, while turning gear is common in American manuals and EPRI reports.

The control side is also identical. Whatever name your P&ID uses, the same permissives, interlocks and shutdown system links apply, and the logic usually lives in the turbine control system or the BPCS rather than the SIS.

Steam Turbine Barring Gear FAQ

What is the purpose of barring gear in a steam turbine?

It turns a hot rotor slowly so it cools and warms evenly without bowing.

A bowed rotor shows high eccentricity, rubs its seals and can even lock in the casing, so barring runs after every trip until the turbine is cool and for at least 4 hours before a start.

What is the difference between barring gear and turning gear in turbines?

There is no difference, since both names describe the same slow rotation gear.

Barring gear is common in India and Europe, while turning gear appears in American manuals and EPRI reports. The permissives, speed range and logic are the same whichever name the drawing uses.

What are the start permissives for a steam turbine barring gear motor?

The usual permissives are lube oil pressure healthy, jacking oil healthy where fitted, rotor at zero speed and pinion engaged.

The steam turbine barring gear motor trips on low lube oil pressure, overload or rotor speed rising above barring speed. Check your OEM logic diagram for the exact switch list.

How do you calculate revolutions and eccentricity ratio on barring step by step?

Multiply barring speed by 60 and by hours to get revolutions, then divide measured eccentricity by the limit.

At 4 rpm for 6 hours the rotor makes 1440 revolutions. With 38 µm against an assumed 50 µm limit the ratio is 76 percent, so the start can go ahead.

What is the normal speed of turning gear on a steam turbine?

EPRI gives a typical range of 2 to 10 rpm, set by the OEM for each machine.

Running below about 2 rpm can damage bearings and cause blade stick slip. Some hydraulic designs turn faster, and EPRI quotes one Siemens system at 20 to 150 rpm.

Why does the barring gear motor trip or fail to engage repeatedly?

Most repeat trips come from a lost permissive, usually low lube oil pressure or a faulty limit switch.

Check pump changeover dips, instrument air to the engage cylinder and motor current. High current points to a rubbing or bowed rotor and needs an eccentricity check before you retry.

What We Learn Today

  • Barring gear turns a hot turbine rotor at about 2 to 10 rpm so it cools evenly and does not bow, rub its seals or lock.
  • The steam turbine barring gear logic engages the pinion only at zero speed with lube and jacking oil healthy, then starts the motor after mesh.
  • Most OEMs need at least 4 hours on barring before steam, and eccentricity must sit inside the OEM limit before the turbine rolls.
